newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Analysts see large potential for Argentina IPOs.
newsitem.headline: Analysts see large potential for Argentina IPOs.

text.p: This year could herald a boom in Argentine initial public offerings and new listings, helped by local pension fund demand, a firm stock market and increasing economic growth, financial analysts say.
"The potential (for IPOs) is enormous this year," said Christopher Ecclestone, chief equity analyst at Interacciones brokerage.
Analysts say the biggest single reason to expect a sharp pickup in IPOs is the increasing appetite for stocks by the local private pension funds, known as AFJPs.
"The market (on the demand side) is more prepared for IPOs than ever before," said Paul Dougall, head of equity sales and trading at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Buenos Aires.
At the end of last year, AFJPs had $864 million invested in stocks. They managed total funds of $5.33 billion at the end of 1996, up from $2.56 billion at the end of 1995.

Based on the recent flow of payments to the funds, Ecclestone reckons some net $100 million will be invested in the stock market by the AFJPs every month in 1997, meaning they have ample funds to put into new issues.

Since the private pension funds were first established in the middle of 1994 they have gradually ventured more into the stock market even though they are still restricted in how much they can invest in stocks.
Now that process is set to speed up, not least because many of the funds have reached the limits they are allowed to invest in any one single stock, explains Ecclestone.
"To maintain their current percentage of funds invested in stocks, it will be difficult for the pension funds not to pick up IPOs," said Hernan Ladeuix, head of equity research at ING Barings.
In addition, analysts say Cresud, Argentina's only listed agribusiness company, which is controlled by billionare investor George Soros, may also go for a capital increase in 1997.
"There might be something on the mining side as well," said Dougall.
Most of all though, the demand by the pension funds opens the way for small firms that previously did not consider an IPO.
"Smaller companies can issue more cheaply" locally, rather than having to go the expensive route of launching ADRs in the United States, said Ecclestone.
"This is a factor (the fund demand) that will make companies favor launching IPOs," said Ladeuix. "I am optimistic for the smaller companies."
Last year only two new Argentine stock issues emerged - an IPO from food retailer Disco and a new issue from steel company Siderar, both of which were successful, said Ladeuix.
